claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by competition between bulk configurational entropy and surface-energy effects.
Bulk configurational entropy favors a single-phase solid solution.
Surface-energy effects drive elemental segregation in high-entropy nanoparticles.
At identical composition and thermal conditions, smaller nanoparticles undergo more surface-energy-driven segregation than larger nanoparticles.
Larger nanoparticles remain more stable as single-phase systems because configurational entropy has a relatively dominant influence.
Nanoparticle size modulates the surface-to-volume ratio.
The size-dependent surface-to-volume ratio influences the balance between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-energy-driven segregation.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility sufficiently to permit segregation.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller particles amplifies surface-energy effects.
Amplified surface-energy effects cause segregation to occur earlier or more strongly in smaller particles.
Under matched high-temperature treatment, approximately 10–20 nm nanoparticles will exhibit more phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity than approximately 50–100 nm nanoparticles.
Approximately 50–100 nm nanoparticles will retain a more stable single-phase structure than approximately 10–20 nm nanoparticles under the same treatment.
The prediction is limited to temperatures at which atomic diffusion is thermally activated.
The prediction is limited to particle-size regimes in which surface effects are significant.
Element-specific segregation tendencies can cause deviations from the predicted size dependence.
The quantitative extent of segregation may differ among high-entropy alloy systems.
